lessons.title: Sinalefa: vowels that meet
lessons.goal: Glide vowels across word boundaries so a phrase sounds like one long word.

tip.title: No gaps between words
tip.body: Spanish doesn't pause between the words of a phrase. When one word ends in a vowel and the next starts with one (h is silent, so it counts as a vowel), the two vowels glide into a single syllable. This is called sinalefa. "Mi amigo" is three syllables, mia-mi-go, not four. "La entrada" → laen-tra-da, "que es" → quees, "todo el día" → to-doel-dí-a, "de España" → dees-pa-ña. Two identical vowels melt into one slightly longer vowel: "va a ir" → vaa-ir, "la amiga" sounds almost like "la miga". English speakers often put a little catch in the throat (a glottal stop, as in "uh-oh") before a word that starts with a vowel. Don't: keep your voice running and move your mouth straight from one vowel to the next. Every vowel keeps its full quality; it just gets shorter. A famous result: "a ver" (let's see) and "haber" (to have) sound identical, and so do "va a ver" (he's going to see) and "va a haber" (there's going to be). Even native speakers mix them up in writing.

phrases.note: A woman's friend: mi amiga. Say it mia-mi-goes-dees-pa-ña.

phrases.t: Va a ir a la oficina.
phrases.n: He's going to go to the office.

lessons.title: Consonant + vowel linking
lessons.goal: Hook a final consonant onto the next word's vowel, and recognise the near-homophones this creates.

tip.title: The consonant jumps to the next word
tip.body: Spanish loves syllables shaped consonant + vowel, and word boundaries don't get in the way. When a word ends in a consonant and the next begins with a vowel (or silent h), the consonant moves over and starts the next syllable: "los otros" → lo-so-tros, "el agua" → e-la-gua, "un hombre" → u-nom-bre, "es así" → e-sa-sí, "más o menos" → má-so-me-nos, "las once" → la-son-ce. So "el hecho" (the fact) sounds exactly like "helecho" (fern), and "las aves" (the birds) like "la sabes" (you know it); context tells them apart. When listening, if you hear lo-so-tros, think "los otros". When speaking, don't stop before the vowel; slide the consonant across. Two traps for English speakers: keep s as a sharp s even between vowels ("los otros" is never "loz otros"), and don't add a glottal catch before the vowel.

phrases.t: Un hombre entró en el bar.
